# fastclick-play-single-mt

Generate traffic using FastClick with throughput and latency measurement

This module supports generating UDP traffic or playing a PCAP.

Both can generate at a given rate (UDP) or acceleration factor (PCAP).
Both can also use a "replay" mode, that is preloading packets in memory then replaying them in loop.

Packets are directed towards one NIC of the "server" role using one NIC of the "client" role and expect to receive packets back on any (eventually the same) NIC.

There is no L3 support (ARP). MAC addresses must be set correctly.

## Usage

Add in your NPF test script:
```bash
%import@client fastclick-play-single-mt
```

### Playing a trace
Be sure to pass the variable `trace=path/to/trace`.
The variable `LIMIT_TIME` will limit the replay time.

### Playing UDP traffic
Give the tag `udpgen` with `--tags udpgen` to the npf command line.
The variable `GEN_LENGTH=128` sets the packet size to 128 bytes. Check the variables section below for other parameters.
The variable `LIMIT_TIME` will limit the replay time.

### Preloading in memory
Give the `replay` tag with `--tags replay` to the npf command line.
The variable `PKTGEN_REPLAY_COUNT=10` will replay 10 times.
The variable `LIMIT_TIME` will limit the replay time instead.

### Packet or bit rate (UDP or trace)
Pass the `rate` tag to express a rate in BPS, `prate` for a rate in PPS.
Then set `GEN_RATE` to define the rate.

### Timing acceleration (traces, replayed or not)
Use `TIMING=0` to play the packets as fast as possible (you might consider preloading in memory, see above).
Use `TIMING=1` to play packets using the original timing, eventually tweaked at X% of the original timing using `TIMING_FNT`.
For instance `TIMING_FNT=200` will replay twice faster. `TIMING_FNT` can be a function of time (given as `x`).
For instance to start replay at 1% at t=0 then 100% at t=10 and then stay at 100%:
```bash
TIMING_FNT=1+min(99,x*10)
```

Arrange the function so the timing is never 0%. At 0% the system will be unscheduled, as the timing is computed for inter-packet time. At 0%, the next packet is never sent so the time stops.

### Replaying from compressed dump (particular cases)
Set `GEN_DUMP=1` (tag `gen_dump`) to use a FromIPSummaryDump instead of FromDump, the trace parameter should therefore follow the FromIPSummaryDump format. Similarly, use `GEN_DUMP=2` (tag `gen_mindump`) to use FromMinDump.

## Zero-loss throughput
Although not tied to this specific module, it is often combined with experimental design to find the zero-loss throughput. The following command line arguments will give the maximum rate a DUT can forward:
```bash
--variables "GEN_RATE=[1000000-16000000#1000000]" --exp-design "zlt(GEN_RATE,PPS,1.01)"
```

## Multi-threading

Pass the variables `GEN_THREADS=X` and `GEN_RX_THREADS=Y` to use X threads for TX and Y threads for RX. Default is 4 for both.

### Multi-threading with traces
The normal way to use multi-threading would be to round-robin the trace between the threads.

By default, each thread will re-read the same trace, which is generally not convenient.

A more efficient way is to use multiple traces pre-split, for instance one trace per thread.
Set `GEN_MULTI_TRACE=N` to use multiple traces, using -1, -2, ... -N suffixes to the trace. If you only have 4 threads (`GEN_THREADS=4`), then only traces from 1 to 4 will be used. Inversely, if you have 4 threads but only two traces, the threads 3 and 4 will fail.

If the `scale_multi_trace` tag is given, then the number of traces is fixed, always sending traces from 1 to `GEN_MULTI_TRACE`. If `GEN_MULTI_TRACE` is smaller than `GEN_THREADS`, some threads will be unused. If `GEN_MULTI_TRACE` is bigger than the number of threads, then they will be distributed in a round-robin fashion. For instance with 16 traces and 4 threads, the first thread will send traces 1, 5, 9 and 13. This tag therefore ensures there is no mismatch between the numbers of traces and threads.

### Deactivate latency to improve performance
Use the `gen_nolat` tag to disable latency tracking. This cannot be done using variables.

### Deactivate packet reception
Use the `gen_norx` tag to disable receiving packets. This will leave CPU resources available for sending.

### Notes on pipeline

The script has a pipelined mode (use the `gen_pipeline` tag which will set `GEN_PIPELINE` to 1) used to ensure only one thread reads from the generator (packet trace, UDP, mindump, etc.). The best option is to pre-split a trace, or use UDP generation that can natively be multi-threaded. Use this as last resort or if you got enough performance without the hassle of splitting the trace.

Source: [`modules/fastclick-play-single-mt.npf`](https://github.com/tbarbette/npf/blob/main/modules/fastclick-play-single-mt.npf)

## Variables

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `PKTGEN_BURST_OUT` | `32` | Number of packet to generate in a burst trade latency accuracy (1) for speed (32) |
| `PKTGEN_REPLAY_COUNT` | `1` | Number of time to replay a trace. Not applicable to UDP |
| `NIC` | `0` | Index of the server NIC the packets are sent to (destination MAC) |
| `CLIENT_NIC` | `0` | Index of the client NIC used as source MAC |
| `RCV_NIC` | `0` | Index of the NIC of this node used to send and receive |
| `LIMIT` | `50000000`<br>`1000000` with `replay` | Maximum number of packets to read |
| `LIMIT_TIME` | `10` | Maximum time to (re)play |
| `GEN_THRESHOLD` | `0` | Do not start measuring latency before reaching that amount of packets per second. Avoids starting computing latency when we receive a random ICMP packets from the switch or something like that |
| `IGNORE` | `0` | Similarly, we can IGNORE the measurement for the X first seconds after the first packet is received. |
| `GEN_THREADS` | `4` | Number of TX threads |
| `GEN_RX_THREADS` | `4` | Number of RX threads |
| `GEN_PIPELINE` | `0`<br>`1` with `gen_pipeline` | Pipelined mode, use the gen_pipeline tag (see above) |
| `GEN_TX_PIPELINE` | `0`<br>`1` with `gen_tx_pipeline` |  |
| `GEN_SOCKET` | `0` | Socket of the NIC |
| `GEN_BURST` | `32` | Maximum amount of packets to read from the NIC |
| `PROMISC` | `false`<br>`true` with `promisc` | Promiscuous mode? |
| `GEN_PAUSE` | `none` | Disable pause frame, set to unset with intel NICs that does not support it |
| `GEN_DESC` | `0` | Number of descriptor, use NIC default with 0 |
| `GEN_CSUM` | `true` | Enable offloaded checksum fixing |
| `END_AFTER` | `0` | Stop reading traces after Xs |
| `GEN_RATE` | `-1`<br>`1000` with `rate` and `prate` | Packet or bitrate, depending on the tag |
| `GEN_RATE_LINK` | `1` |  |
| `LATENCYDUMP` | `/tmp/latency.csv` | File where to dump the individual latency of all packets |
| `ITERATION_TIME` | `0`<br>`1` with `iterative` | Iterative mode |
| `GEN_MULTI_TRACE` | `0`<br>`1` with `gen_multi_trace` | Use multiple trace (for multi-threading, see above) |
| `GEN_FORCE_ETHER` | `0`<br>`1` with `trace_is_ip` | Force ethernet encapsulation |
| `GEN_DUMP` | `0`<br>`1` with `gen_dump`<br>`2` with `gen_mindump`<br>`-1` with `udpgen` | Packet generation mode, use tags instead of tweaking this |
| `GEN_LENGTH` | `64` with `udpgen` | Packet size in bytes, with the udpgen tag |
| `GEN_SEQUENTIAL` | `1` | Generate sequential UDP ports instead of random. This is actually much faster. |
| `GEN_RX` | `1`<br>`0` with `gen_norx` | Enable RX |
| `TIMING` | `1` with `timing` | Use the timing of the trace, see above |
| `TIMING_FNT` | `100` with `timing` | Speed of the replay in percent of the original timing, can be a function of the time x (see above) |
| `GEN_START_DELAY` | `5` | Delay trace start |
| `NUMBEROFFSET` | `40` | Where to put the latency record in the packet |
